replying_to: Replying to Seq2Tok: Deep Sequence Tokenizer for Retrieval
display_title: Official Review of Paper2948 by Reviewer BBHm

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of information retrieval that searches similar items to a given query. The paper introduces a new tokenizer and claims that Seq2Tok can convert a continuous sequence (e.g. audio) to discrete tokens. The purpose of the conversion is to enable easier retrieval. The paper conducts extensive experiments and claims that Seq2Tok achieves consistent performance on audio retrieval tasks.
content.main_review:
Main Review

The paper tries to introduce a new method, called Seq2Tok, to convert a continuous sequence to discrete tokens. The new method is evaluated extensively in the experiment section. Results show that Seq2Tok achieves impressive performance that outperforms several existing methods (see Table 1). However, the paper lacks explanations on why Seq2Tok is superior. The current draft contains many mathematic formulas and tables, but none of them are about the input data format, output format, and baseline methods. It is difficult for readers to understand the baseline methods and the contributions of the work over baselines.   


Pros:

1. The paper presents a new method that converts a continuous sequence to discrete tokens to simplify similarity search. The design of the method is reasonable that takes sequence pairs to train a neural network. When the neural network is well trained, it can be used to project every continuous sequence to discrete tokens. 
 

2. The proposed method achieves impressive performance. According to Table 1, Seq2tok outperforms a weak baseline by a large margin. For example, Seq2tok achieves 0.84 in row TokB DTW and column Normal V, while the baseline Triplet DTW achieves only 0.278 under the same setting. In addition, Seq2tok can outperform strong baselines. For example, under the above setting Seq2tok achieves 0.84, which outperforms the 0.75 of Wav2Vec 2.0 DTW. 


Cons: 

1.	The presentation of the paper is not clear. For example, table 1 is difficult to understand. Some numbers are marked in bold but the table caption does not explain why. Are numbers in bold mean good performance? The paper should explain that. Also, there are many undefined terms including “Normal”, “V”, “TS”, “PS”, “DTW” and “Compressed”. It will be good if the paper can define these terms formally in the paper or use other terms that are known by the public. 

2.	The technical contribution of the paper remains unknown. The paper lacks a background section between Related Work and Methodology. The background section is necessary because it explains the logic of baselines. Without knowing the data processing flows of baselines, it is hard to understand the technical contributions of the paper. 


3.	The performance of seq2tok is unstable. In table 1, it seems seq2tok does not always outperform baseline Wav2Vaec 2.0. For example, the numbers In row TokA ED are always smaller than numbers in row Wav2Vec 2.0 DTW. It will be good if the paper can explain why.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has merits that introduce a new method to project a continuous sequence (e.g. audio) to discrete tokens. However, it is unclear whether the new method advances existing methods. The paper should add one paragraph in the Introduction section to articulate the contributions explicitly.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2948 by Reviewer BBHm

content.title: Rebuttal to Reviewer BBHm
content.comment:
The presentation of the paper is not clear. For example, table 1 is difficult to understand. Some numbers are marked in bold but the table caption does not explain why. Are numbers in bold mean good performance? The paper should explain that. Also, there are many undefined terms including “Normal”, “V”, “TS”, “PS”, “DTW” and “Compressed”. It will be good if the paper can define these terms formally in the paper or use other terms that are known by the public. 

Rebuttal: The numbers marked in bold mean good performance. 

The terms mean as follows:

V - Vanilla query (no augmentation applied to query)

TS - Time Stretched query

PS- Pitch Shifted query

DTW- all models with the term DTW beside them indicate that the scores in the corresponding rows are for DTW based similarity Search

Compressed- We introduced a compression strategy in section 3.4 of the manuscript. In all the tables, we have presented the performance of compressed sequences of representations and tokens in the "Compressed" column.

Note all these terms have been introduced in the Results subsection of section 4.4. of the manuscript.

    The technical contribution of the paper remains unknown. The paper lacks a background section between Related Work and Methodology. The background section is necessary because it explains the logic of baselines. Without knowing the data processing flows of baselines, it is hard to understand the technical contributions of the paper. 

Rebuttal: There are no existing published works on the problem we worked on. Our work is the first one tackling this interesting problem. The baselines we have used are not designed specifically to solve our problem but all have desirable qualities which made us choose them to evaluate the performance of our models. We did present the theory relating to our baselines in section 4.2 of the manuscript.

    The performance of seq2tok is unstable. In table 1, it seems seq2tok does not always outperform baseline Wav2Vaec 2.0. For example, the numbers In row TokA ED are always smaller than numbers in row Wav2Vec 2.0 DTW. It will be good if the paper can explain why. 

Rebuttal: In Wav2Vec 2.0 DTW, we are performing DTW based similarity search. The query is a sequence of representation vectors and the search database is filled with sequences of representation vectors.  
In TokA ED (Seq2Tok trained using Approach A), we are performing Edit Distance-based similarity search. The query is a sequence of discrete tokens and the search database is filled with sequences of discrete tokens.

A sequence of representations vectors has more information than a sequence of discrete tokens. Hence, although there is a speedup obtained by representing the audio as a sequence of tokens there is a trade-off in search performance.

replying_to: Replying to Seq2Tok: Deep Sequence Tokenizer for Retrieval
display_title: Official Review of Paper2948 by Reviewer dyUG

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a data-driven tokenizer whose goal is to convert a continual-valued (raw) sequence into a sequence of tokens. The proposed tokenizer is trained from pairs of raw sequences and token sequences, without any pre-defined tokens.
content.main_review:
Pros:
+ The proposed data-driven tokenizer trained from the pairs of semantically similar sequences is novel and helps to improve the performance on sequence retrieval tasks in the speech domain.

+ This paper provides extensive experiments on three tasks (query by humming, speech search, and keyword spotting) with ablation studies to prove the superiority of the proposed method.

Concerns:
- The concern about this paper is the generalizability of the proposed method. That is, the proposed method is mainly designed to solve sequence retrieval tasks in the speech domain. According to that, this paper tries to minimize the edit distance between two token sequences as the objective of the proposed method. Even most sequence retrieval tasks in the speech domain are applied to this formulation, however, all sequence retrieval tasks are not regarded as the edit distance minimization like similarity text retrieval task.

- In the introduction, this paper insists that the proposed method can be used for text search methods. However, the proposed tokenizer is not applicable to a sentence or document tokenization because many tokenizers used in NLP tasks do not suppose that query and target sequences have a one-to-one mapping relationship. (e.g. subword tokenizer is not an one-to-one mapping between a raw sequence (sentence) and a sequence of tokens (subwords)). Nevertheless, the proposed tokenizer supposes that query and token sequence are one-to-one mapping.

- The paper is diffciult to follow. The motivation of the proposed method “relevant landmarks appear in the same order in both sequences” is not clearly intuitive. Giving some examples would make a reader easy to understand intuitively.

- The proposed method is highly dependent on pairs of semantically similar feature sequences. In a practical situation, it is questionable how to collect these “semantically” similar sequences.

- The baselines used in the experiments do not utilize the pairs of similar sequences to train their models. The reviewer thinks that this comparison seems unfair because the proposed method is trained with more information derived from the pairs of semantically similar sequences.

- The title of this paper is “Seq2Tok: deep sequence tokenizer for retrieval”. The title is too general to specify the proposed method because the proposed method is valid for “sequence” retrieval tasks in the “speech” domain. It would be better to change the title to focus on the main part of the proposed method.

- In “Transformer as Encoder” experiments, the performances of “TokB + Trans” are worse than ones of the BiLSTM model. However, BiLSTM is required to read all sequences, but Transformer is not. It would be better to show the speed comparison.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed data-driven tokenizer is novel, but the manuscript is too general and experiments are not convincing.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2948 by Reviewer dyUG

content.title: Rebuttal to Reviewer dyUG
content.comment:
“The concern ... task.” 

Rebuttal: Our proposed tokenizer takes a sequence of vectors as input. The encoder module given the input sequence outputs a sequence of representations of same length as input sequence. The vector quantizer module given the representation sequence outputs a sequence of tokens of same length as input sequence (hence, each vector in the input sequence is mapped to a token).  

We presented the performance of our encoder-generated representations in DTW-based similarity search too. 
As a result, our method can also be used for DTW-based similarity retrieval tasks. 

We can also extend our proposed method to sequence retrieval tasks in the domain of videos. Video is a sequence of image frames and each image frame can be represented as a single vector using CNNs, as a result, videos can be represented as a sequence of vectors. 
Our method can be used in any sequence retrieval task which involves sequences of vectors.  

In Section 5: Conclusion and Future Work in our manuscript , we have mentioned that we are also aiming to extend the proposed framework to 2D data retrieval. 

      In the introduction, ... mapping. 

Rebuttal: This is a preliminary step towards sequence tokenization with the assumption that query sequence and token sequence are one-to-one mapping (hence are of the same length). In future work, we aim to remove this assumption of one-to-one mapping. 

In this manuscript, we observed the performance of compressed token sequences (obtained via consecutive duplicate deletion) and presented the results in the "Compressed" column in all the performance tables 1,3,4,5,6. We also presented a sequence compression technique in section 3.4 where the query sequence of vectors (mapped to a sequence of representations) is compressed to a smaller sequence of vectors given the token sequence and presented their performances in the "Compressed" columns of the performance tables.

     The paper ...intuitively. 

Rebuttal: Say we have two recordings of the word ‘cat’ spoken by two different persons. 
The word cat has three phonemes in the following order - /c/ + /a/ + /t/.
Whatever differences there may be in pitch and time stretch amongst the two recordings, the three phonemes /c/, /a/, /t/ occur in the same order (/c/ + /a/ + /t/) in both the recordings. 
Here to recognize that the two recordings are similar, our model must identify landmarks in the feature representations of the recordings which encode the occurrences of the phonemes /c/, /a/, and /t/. Such landmarks might not summarise melodic information such as pitch information. The tokens generated by our model will encode phonetic information. 

Now let there be two recordings of a particular song sung by two different persons.  One person might sing out the whole song along with the lyrics while another might hum out the melody of the song. Here to recognize that the two recordings are similar, our model must identify landmarks in the feature representations of the recordings which summarise melodic information such as pitch information, occurrences of notes. The tokens generated by our model will then encode melodic information. 

    The proposed ... sequences. 

Rebuttal: For search tasks like QBSH, KWS, QBE, Search-by-Example collecting semantically similar sequences is very easy. We also presented in our manuscript ( Section 4.4 - Token Semantics ) the performance of our tokenizer when it is trained with pairs of sequences that are not semantically similar (name of model - TokB+NoSim). It still outperformed the baselines although there is a drop in robustness. 

    The baselines ... sequences. 
 
Rebuttal: MIPS and Triplet Models are fed with semantically similar pairs of sequences (x,x'). 
All originals (MIPS) and anchors (Triplet) are sampled from x. 
For the t_th element in x, similar element (augmented replicas In MIPS and positive samples in Triplet) is randomly sampled from the set of elements in x' with index in the range [t-w, t+w] where w is a constant (5 for MIR-QBSH and 1 for TIMIT).

Wav2vec 2.0 and Wav2vec Tok do not use semantically similar pairs of sequences.

    The title ... method. 

Rebuttal: As suggested by the reviewer, we changed the title of the paper to “Wav2Tok: Deep sequence Tokenizer for Audio Retrieval” .

    In “Transformer ... comparison. 

Rebuttal: In our search experiments, our query sequence is compared with all the sequences present in the search database and then a ranking over the sequences in the database is formed based on similarity (in descending order of similarity) to the query. We used transformer as the encoder module of our tokenizer in the experiment. The dimensionality of the generated representations is the same for both BiLSTM and Transformer encoders, the search time for DTW-based similarity search is more or less the same. For Edit distance based search,

 TokB+Trans - 0.368 secs (normal) 0.08 (compressed)
 
TokB - 0.32 secs (normal) 0.04 (compressed)

display_title: Official Review of Paper2948 by Reviewer 37Kx

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to speed up search for similar sequences in cases where data is continuous valued and similar sequence search is computationally expensive.  It proposes to convert continuous valued sequence to a sequence of discrete tokens.  The token vocabulary and assignment of features to tokens is constructed via k-means clustering and evolves during the model training process.  
Results are presented on two tasks: QBSH (query by singing/humming) and TIMIT speech search and keyword spotting, demonstrating that the proposed approach yields better results as compared to baseline DTW methods, and is also more robust to input distortions.  However a comparison with previously published results is missing.
content.main_review:
Pros:

a) Significant speed up in similar sequence search.

Cons:

a) The technical presentation and formulations in the paper are difficult to follow.  For instance:
* The problem statement in Section 3.1 is incomplete.  Simply requiring that edit distance is minimized can be trivially achieved by mapping all sequences to a fixed token sequence.
* Model training happens by concatenating encoder generated feature vectors for similar input samples (if I follow it correctly), tokenizing these vectors, and then creating prototypes for tokens.  It is not clear how this imposes the constraint that similar sequences should generate same sequence of tokens in same order so that edit distance between token sequences for similar samples is minimized.  That is, what is the inductive bias in this training procedure that leads the model to hypothesize similar token sequences for similar input samples.  Perhaps there is a lack in my understanding to the training procedure, please clarify.
* Did the authors try approaches that more directly aim to minimize the token edit distance between similar sequences?
* Initial centroids for the tokenizer are estimated via k-means clustering of features generated by a freshly initialized encoder.  Wouldn’t it be better to estimate the centroids (at least association of features to centroids) based on input features that are not processed by a randomly initialized network?

b) In the baseline approaches
* For MIPS it is stated that model is trained with an augmented replica.  Unclear why an augmented replica is being generated when similar pairs of samples are known.
* In Wav2Vec2.0 approach it is also not clear how the pairs of similar samples are being utilized, how are the distractor features being obtained.  A more detailed description is needed.

c) The experimental results are not compared with previously published results, making it very hard to determine the value of proposed approach.

Relatively minor edits:
* What is ’s’ in paragraph after Eq. (5)
* z^{org} in MIPS baseline needs to be defined
content.summary_of_the_review:
My rating is based on:

a) Lack of clarity and precision in presentation.  As discussed above, the problem statement is incomplete and the inductive bias in the proposed model needs to be made clear.  Also description of few baselines as they relate to the task of similar sequence retrieval is unclear.

b) Lack of comparison with previously published results to put the proposed approach in context.

content.title: Rebuttal to Reviewer 37Kx
content.comment:
* The problem ... sequence. 

 
Rebuttal:  We have changed our problem statement to , 

Given a pair of semantically similar feature sequences $(\mathcal{X}_i, \mathcal{X}_j)$ of length $T_i$ and $T_j$ respectively and feature sequence $\mathcal{X}_k$ of length $T_k$ with no similarity to either of the feature sequences $\mathcal{X}_i$ or $\mathcal{X}_j$, we aim to map sequence $\mathcal{X}_i$ to sequence of tokens $\mathcal{T}_i$ of length $T_i'\leq T_i$, sequence $\mathcal{X}_j$ to sequence of tokens $\mathcal{T}_j$ of length $T_j' \leq T_j$, and sequence $\mathcal{X}_k$ to sequence of tokens $\mathcal{T}_k$ of length $T_k' \leq T_k$ where all the tokens belong to a finite alphabet $\mathbb{A}$ such that, the edit distance between  $\mathcal{T}_i$ and $\mathcal{T}_j$ is minimum while that between $\mathcal{T}_k$ and $\mathcal{T}_i$ as well as $\mathcal{T}_k$ and $\mathcal{T}_j$ is maximum.


* Model ... clarify. 
  
Rebuttal: Our loss function has no term which explicitly imposes the constraint that similar sequences should generate same sequence of tokens in same order so that edit distance between token sequences for similar samples is minimized. 

This is a preliminary step towards solving our problem. In future works, we aim to design a training procedure which explicitly imposes a constraint which leads the model to hypothesize similar token sequence for similar input sequences. 


* Did the authors... sequences? 

Rebuttal: This a new and interesting problem. We did not find any previously published works solving this problem. 

* Initial centroids ... network? 

Rebuttal: The main motivation of our method is to think of the tokenizer as an agent experiencing the audio as sequence of feature vectors.  The encoder module of the tokenizer generates context from the input sequence. It inputs each vector in the input sequence and outputs a contextualized representation vector. The constraint of L-2 normalization on the representation vectors makes the context space spherical. A spherical k-means vector quantizer then segments the spherical space into K segments corresponding to K tokens belonging to a finite alphabet and maps the contextualized representation vector to any one of the tokens. 

 

 Our training procedure requires the vector quantizer module to perform perfect clustering in the context space generated by the encoder.  

In TokB+newInit, we applied k-means clustering on the input features which resulted in a labelling of each of the input feature vectors. Given the cluster memberships of the input feature vectors, we calculated the initial centroids with the corresponding encoder generated representation vectors.  

 The following table presents the results of TokB+newInit in comparison to TokB.  





|  Model                    ||       Normal                           ||   Compressed                      |

|                                || V       |  TS  |  PS    | TS+PS || V        |  TS  |  PS  | TS+PS | 

| TokB DTW              ||  0.84 | 0.8   | 0.825| 0.753    || 0.722 | 0..64| 0.68 | 0.57     |

|TokB+newInit DTW || 0.83   | 0.77 | 0.81  | 0.74      || 0.68   | 0.5    | 0.59| 0.47     |   

| TokB ED                 || 0.768| 0.741| 0.75 | 0.77      ||0.63    | 0.54  | 0.54| 0.48     |

|TokB+newInit ED    || 0.71   | 0.57  | 0.68  | 0.5       ||0.53    | 0.38  | 0.45| 0.35     |


[Note: V – Vanilla query, TS- Time stretched query, PS- pitch Shifted query 

Search database- Validation split 

Query sampled from Test split] 

Although the representations generated by TokB+newInit give comparable performance in DTW based search. The quality of tokenization performed by TokB+newInit is poor and not robust to the different augmentations applied to query.  
The initial centroids in TokB+newInit do not cluster the spherical context space generated by the encoder properly. As a result, training with such initial centroids resulted in degradation in the quality of tokenization. 


* For ... known.

Rebuttal: MIPS and Triplet Models are fed with semantically similar pairs of sequences (x,x'). All originals (MIPS) and anchors (Triplet) are sampled from x. For the t_th element in x, similar element (augmented replicas in MIPS and positive samples in Triplet) is randomly sampled from the set of elements in x' with index in the range [t-w, t+w] where w is a constant (5 for MIR-QBSH and 1 for TIMIT).

* In Wav2Vec2.0 ... needed.

Rebuttal: Pairs of similar sequences are not being utilized in training Wav2Vec2.0.

The distractor samples for time step t are sampled from all other time steps in the same utterance.
 
* The experimental results are not compared with previously published results, making it very hard to determine the value of proposed approach.

Rebuttal: This is a new and very interesting problem. There are no previously published works solving our problem.


*  What is ’s’ in paragraph after Eq. (5)

Answer: We have resolved the typing error. It is \tau not s.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2948 by Reviewer cfU5

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an algorithm to do sequence matching using a tokenizations of the original sequences, and evaluates it in three different settings. The test environments are non-standard setups of public databases, with a closed vocabulary of sequences, i.e. training, validation, and testing sets contain the same sequences.
content.main_review:
Strenghts
-------------
The paper approaches an interesting problem, how to effectively search over sequences such as raw audio in an efficient way, by learning quantized representations that specifically take into account the sequence similarity problem (rather than just a frame-based criterion)

Weaknesses
-----------------
The description of the work is very dense and often confusing. Authors employ three test sets, three baselines, and multiple variants of the proposed system, but as none of these correspond to known and established configurations, I do not have a sense if the proposed approach does well, or not. Despite that variability (and the corresponding density in the descriptions), it seems that the test set actually only contains sequences that were seen during training - so I cannot tell if the algorithm would be able to classify an unseen input sequence reasonably well, or not. This generalization ability is an indispensable requirement for a meaningful contribution to sequence classification, because otherwise we could simply do closed-set classification.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper tackles an interesting problem, and has interesting ideas, but the presentation is too dense to be useful, the experimental setup is not standard, and the results are therefore not likely to be of interest to the general audience. I can therefore not recommend acceptance of this paper.

display_title: Our model can generalize to unseen sequences

content.title: Our model can generalize to unseen sequences
content.comment:
There are no existing published works on the problem we worked on. Our work is the first one tackling this interesting problem. The baselines we have used are not designed specifically to solve our problem but all have desirable qualities which made us choose them to evaluate the performance of our models.

Our model can generalize well to unseen sequences. 
We conducted another experiment as follows to validate our statement:

The MIR-QBSH dataset is composed of 4431 humming or singing recordings each corresponding to any one of the 48 songs in the dataset. 

We trained our model TokB with recordings each corresponding to any one of 40 out of 48 songs in dataset and evaluated our model's performance on recordings corresponding to any one of the remaining 8 songs. 

All recordings are converted to STFT matrices and hence to sequences of feature vectors. 

Number of sequences in search database - 167 (each corresponding to any one of the 8 unseen songs)
 
Number of queries- 225 (each corresponding to any one of the 8 unseen songs)


The search results (MRR scores) for the proposed TokB method are as follows:

* DTW based similarity Search:

Vanilla Query (no augmentations applied to query) - 0.89

Time Stretched Query - 0.86

Pitch Shifted Query - 0.87

Time Stretched + Pitch Shifted Query - 0.83

* Edit Distance based similarity Search:

Vanilla Query (no augmentations applied to query) - 0.79

Time Stretched Query - 0.71

Pitch Shifted Query - 0.763

Time Stretched + Pitch Shifted Query - 0.7


* DTW based similarity Search on Compressed Sequences:

Vanilla Query (no augmentations applied to query) - 0.86

Time Stretched Query - 0.764

Pitch Shifted Query - 0.8

Time Stretched + Pitch Shifted Query - 0.7

* Edit Distance based similarity Search on Compressed Sequences:

Vanilla Query (no augmentations applied to query) - 0.77

Time Stretched Query - 0.7

Pitch Shifted Query - 0.73

Time Stretched + Pitch Shifted Query - 0.622

These results on unseen target songs are very similar to those achieved by TokB in Table 1, supporting that TokB is able to generalize well on unseen targets.
